nameStory: Wilson's Storm-Petrel honors Alexander Wilson, a Scottish-American ornithologist who helped pioneer bird studies in early America. The 'storm-petrel' part comes from sailors' observations of these tiny seabirds that seem to dance across storm-tossed waves, appearing almost magically during rough weather.
description: Wilson's Storm-Petrel is a small, dark seabird about the size of a sparrow that spends most of its life far out at sea. These remarkable little birds have sooty-black plumage with a distinctive white rump patch that flashes as they flutter and dance across the ocean waves. They're one of the most abundant bird species in the world, though most people never see them since they live their lives on the open ocean. During summer, they migrate thousands of miles from their Antarctic breeding grounds to feed in North Atlantic waters.

idTips.label: White rump patch
idTips.description: A bright white, U-shaped patch at the base of the tail that contrasts sharply with the dark body - this flashes conspicuously as the bird flies and is visible from considerable distance

idTips.label: Dancing flight pattern
idTips.description: Flutters and patters across the water surface with legs dangling, appearing to walk on water as it picks at plankton - looks like a bat or large butterfly over the waves

idTips.label: Overall dark coloration
idTips.description: Sooty black or dark brown all over except for the white rump, with no white markings on wings or underparts when seen up close

idTips.label: Small size
idTips.description: Sparrow-sized seabird, much smaller than gulls or other common ocean birds, with relatively long, narrow wings for its tiny body

idTips.label: Yellow webbed feet
idTips.description: Bright yellow feet with black webs between the toes, often visible as the bird patters across the water surface while feeding

habitat: You'll only encounter Wilson's Storm-Petrels far offshore in New England waters, typically 10+ miles from land in deep ocean areas. They're occasionally spotted from whale-watching boats, ferries to islands, or during pelagic birding trips that specifically venture into deep water. Very rarely, storms may blow exhausted individuals close to shore or even inland.

seasonality.spring: Begin arriving in New England waters in late spring as they migrate north from Antarctic breeding grounds, though still quite far offshore and rarely seen.
seasonality.summer: Most abundant in New England waters during summer months when they're actively feeding in nutrient-rich areas, following whale-watching boats for churned-up prey.
seasonality.fall: Still present in early fall but gradually moving back toward southern oceans, with peak numbers often in late summer before migration.
seasonality.winter: Absent from New England waters - they've returned to the Southern Hemisphere where they breed during the austral summer.

funFact: Wilson's Storm-Petrels make one of the longest migrations on Earth, traveling roughly 44,000 miles annually from their Antarctic breeding colonies to northern waters and back - that's nearly twice around the entire planet every single year!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with Leach's Storm-Petrel, but Wilson's has a square or slightly notched tail (not deeply forked), yellow feet (not black), and a more fluttery flight pattern. Remember: Wilson's walks on water, Leach's swoops and dives.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'petrels,' storm-petrels are not closely related to the larger petrels and shearwaters. The name comes from Saint Peter walking on water, referencing their ability to appear to run across the ocean surface. These are truly oceanic birds - they only come to land to breed on remote islands.
compareHints: Wilson's Storm-Petrel is the only member of its genus in New England waters, making it unique among local storm-petrels. Compared to other storm-petrels in the region, Wilson's is distinguished by its square tail, yellow feet, and more direct flight with frequent water-pattering. Other storm-petrels tend to have forked tails, different colored feet, and more erratic flight patterns.
